newsitem.title: UK: Stubborn UK retail prices rule against rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Stubborn UK retail prices rule against rate cut.

text.p: Core UK retail price inflation failed to fall for the fourth month in a row in August, leaving the chances of another interest rate cut looking slim at best, analysts said on Thursday.
"The figures are a little worse than expected but that's largely due to a spike in petrol prices," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
"Both Clarke and George could use these figures to justify their case but basically we see no change in interest rates for the foreseeable future," Shepperd said.

Underlying retail price inflation held steady at 2.8 percent year-on-year in August. It has stuck there since May and is at the same level it was in the middle of last year. Economists had forecast it would edge down to 2.7 percent.

Headline inflation continued its steady drift downwards on an annual basis, dropping to 2.1 percent year-on-year, from 2.2 in July. But both the headline and core rates showed chunky monthly increases.
"Underlying inflation failed to fall as many had expected," said Andrew Snowball, economist at the Cooperative Bank. "That should nip any speculation of yet another rate cut in the bud."
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke pushed through a quarter-point rate cut in June against the wishes of Bank of England governor Eddie George.
With elections due to be held by May 1997, analysts say Clarke may try to sneak in another reduction regardless of the Bank's opposition.
Shepperd said official interest rates would probably stick at 5.75 percent for the foreseeable future.
He said rising petrol prices, which helped force motoring costs up by 1.0 percent in August, were largely to blame for sticky retail prices but were not of undue concern.
"Underlying inflation trend is on a flat trend at worst. Trends in wage settlements underline the view that there's little stirring on the inflation front."
Snowball was more worried about latent inflation pressures.

He noted seasonal food prices pushed year-on-year inflation down even though they jumped 5.3 percent on the month. In August last year, seasonal food prices were 13.1 percent up year-on-year as a hot summer took its toll.
"Seasonal food price rises from a year ago dropped out of the index...but they have been replaced by other things, such as higher clothing and footwear prices," Snowball said.
Clothing and footwear prices jumped 1.5 percent in August.

David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy, conceded the figures were a little above forecast but said all was not doom and gloom. He said many of the price rises in August were reactions to sharp falls in July -- clothing and footwear prices fell 4.9 percent in July, for instance.
He said the acid test will come in the months ahead. "It is not clear that retailers are at the stage where they feel confident about expanding margins through higher prices."
"The key test of consumers' willingness to pay more will come as the summer sales discounts are fully unwound," he said.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said higher petrol prices would be likely to be sustained in the months ahead.
"It delays rather than completely eliminates the scope for inflation to fall in coming months," he said. "I think interest rates are firmly on hold."
